text:
I keep coming back to a slightly unfashionable thought: building the thing is often the easy part.

This week my team published three pieces that all sit one step beyond the asset itself.

First, African trade corridors. A road or railway can be complete on paper while firms still hit customs delays, unreliable power, slow payments and standards that stop at the border. Financially, that means expensive infrastructure can underperform because the operating system around it is fragmented. Ethically, it matters because smaller firms and workers are usually least able to absorb those frictions. Regional integration only means much if it changes who can actually trade and produce.

https://stonecomms.com/research/border-inside-factory-africa-production-systems

Cold chain is similar. The obvious answer to food loss is to install a cold room. But a technically good cold room can still sit empty if there is no reliable product flow, buyer, operator, affordable tariff or working capital. The investment issue is utilisation: capital should buy a useful service, not an impressive machine. The human issue is bargaining power. Cooling only helps farmers, fishers and traders if the extra time gives them better options rather than another cost.

https://stonecomms.com/research/hour-after-harvest-africa-cold-chain-service-design

Then nature-based infrastructure. Mangroves, wetlands and floodplains can protect ports, roads and communities, but they are often treated as environmental projects sitting beside infrastructure rather than part of the protective service. Financially, that creates a familiar risk: everyone funds establishment and nobody funds stewardship. Ethically, it also forces harder questions about land, fishing, grazing and who pays the cost of keeping the system working.

https://stonecomms.com/research/infrastructure-with-roots-africa-nature-based-resilience

The thread through all three is not especially glamorous: interfaces, operators, maintenance, rights and accountability. But those are often the things that decide whether infrastructure creates value after the ribbon is cut.

Coming up, my team is looking at another version of the same problem: climate maps are getting better, but do they actually change budgets, projects and operating decisions?
